  Two things bite here. Sign convention: the log risk ratio below is vaccinated-versus-control, so NEGATIVE means the vaccine helped; some metafor examples reverse the arms and print +0.7145 for the same data. And I-squared has two standard definitions that differ by about a tenth of a percentage point on this dataset -- axiom reports the Q-based one, metafor's rma() prints the model-based one.

df for Q: axiom 12, published 12

A word about that I^2, because the first run of this file looked like a bug.
    axiom's heterogeneity() returns the Q-BASED I^2, (Q - df) / Q = 0.9212.
    metafor's rma() prints the MODEL-BASED one, tau^2 / (tau^2 + s^2) = 0.9222,
    where s^2 is Higgins & Thompson's typical within-study variance.

    They differ by 0.0010 here -- small enough to look like a rounding
    error and large enough to be worth chasing. Neither is wrong; they answer
    slightly different questions. What would have been wrong is quietly widening
    the tolerance until the table went green.

as a risk ratio: 0.489  [0.344, 0.696]
  the vaccine cut tuberculosis risk by about 51% on average

but I^2 is 92%, so 'on average' is carrying a lot of weight.
  interval on the MEAN effect     [-1.108, -0.321]
  interval for the NEXT trial     [-2.009, +0.580]
  as risk ratios                  [0.13, 1.79]
  A new trial could plausibly see almost no benefit. That is not noise --
  it is the trials genuinely disagreeing, and it is the finding.

split by absolute latitude, the classic moderator:
  within 35 degrees of equator   k= 7  log RR -0.265  RR 0.77
  further than 35 degrees        k= 6  log RR -1.197  RR 0.30
  Two very different vaccines, or one vaccine and two very different settings.

Egger's test: intercept -2.112 (p = 0.189)

most influential trials when dropped (shift in pooled-se units):
  Hart & Sutherland           -0.479
  TPT Madras                  +0.446
  Comstock et al              +0.350

Reading it
    Every published quantity reproduced. That is the claim worth making: not that
    axiom's formulas are self-consistent -- the unit tests already cover that --
    but that running this library end to end on somebody else's data lands where
    somebody else's software landed.

    The substantive reading is the second half. A pooled risk ratio around 0.49
    looks decisive until you notice I-squared above 90% and a prediction interval
    that reaches almost to 1.0. The average of thirteen trials that disagree this
    much is a number about the thirteen trials, not about the vaccine.

Reading it
    Both certified parameters recovered to about one part in ten thousand, with
    the certified values inside the 95% intervals, and a residual sum of squares
    that sits just above the certified minimum rather than below it.

    That last point is the one worth dwelling on. A fit that reported a LOWER
    residual sum of squares than NIST's certified optimum would not be a better
    fit -- it would be a bug, either in the model being fitted or in the arithmetic
    reporting it. Benchmarks with certified answers catch that class of error,
    which is exactly why NIST publishes them.

    What axiom adds beyond the certified numbers is the last table: NIST reports
    two parameters and their standard deviations, and axiom will also tell you what
    the curve does at a pressure of 1200 and how sure it is.

  Gender is one of the strongest predictors in this survey, and a confounder
  three times stronger still does not overturn the sign. That is a much more
  useful sentence than a p-value, and it is falsifiable: name such a variable.

specification                       estimate       se
no covariates at all                  0.0634   0.0197
covariates, no village effects        0.0489   0.0184
published specification               0.0973   0.0233
  The village effects are doing real work. Which specification is right is
  a question about the world -- were attacks indiscriminate WITHIN villages? --
  and no amount of fitting settles it.

Reading it
    The published coefficient and standard error come back from the raw survey to
    four decimal places, and the sensitivity numbers built on them match the paper.
    That is the end-to-end claim: not that a formula is implemented correctly, but
    that the whole path from 1,276 rows to a published sensitivity analysis runs
    through this library and arrives in the same place.

    The substantive point is the one Cinelli and Hazlett were making. This design
    cannot rule out confounding, and no design of this kind can. What it can do is
    state precisely how strong a confounder would have to be, benchmark that
    against a variable everyone can picture, and let a reader decide. That is a
    claim someone can argue with, which is more than significance offers.

  randomized sample : 445 people (185 treated, 260 control)

  published                $1,794
  difference               $0.34

  adjusting for covariates anyway: $1,676 (se 639)
  Barely moves, which is what randomization is supposed to buy: the
  covariates were already balanced, so conditioning on them changes little.

  The randomized arms match. The PSID group is a different population:
  older, better educated, and earning an order of magnitude more before
  the programme even started.

OBSERVATIONAL VERSION: 185 treated vs 2,490 PSID controls

specification                               estimate        se    vs truth
experimental benchmark                         1,794       633           0
PSID controls, no adjustment                 -15,205     1,155     -16,999
PSID controls, 8 covariates                      752       915      -1,042

  The unadjusted observational estimate says the programme destroyed
  earnings. Controlling for everything available recovers some of it and
  still misses the benchmark badly. Both regressions are correctly
  computed; both answer a question other than the one asked.

What the identification layer says, from the graph alone:
  randomized   : identified via backdoor, adjust for nothing
  observational: downgraded (backdoor_unmeasured), needs ['motivation'] which is not in the file
  'motivation' stands for whatever led a person to enrol. It is not a
  variable anyone collected, and it is the whole problem.

sensitivity of the observational estimate ($752):
  to bring it to zero, a confounder needs partial R2 of 1.6% in both
  to move it the $1,042 to the benchmark, it needs 2.2%
  Here we happen to know the answer, because the experiment was run. In
  every real application you do not, which is why the number to report is
  the strength required rather than the estimate alone.

Reading it
    axiom reproduces the experimental benchmark to the dollar: $1,794
    against a published $1,794. That is the part this file
    checks.

    The part it demonstrates is older and more important. Two analyses of the same
    treated people, differing only in who they were compared against, disagree by
    thousands of dollars and in sign. No diagnostic run on the observational data
    flags it, because nothing is wrong with the arithmetic. The randomized
    benchmark is the only reason anyone knows which answer was wrong -- and it
    exists here only because somebody ran the experiment.

    That is the argument for the whole first pillar: decide whether the data can
    answer the question BEFORE fitting, because afterwards it looks fine either
    way.
